content.text: {"relation": "REFINED", "consensus_summary": "A sign ('oth/semeion) is a perceptible act, event, or object — most characteristically a miraculous work — that points beyond itself to God's presence and power, authenticating His messenger and revealing divine identity (paradigmatically Jesus' Johannine signs), with secondary senses including covenant markers, eschatological portents, prophetic sign-acts, and confirmatory tokens.", "book_summary": "A sign is a prophecy given in advance — frequently embodied in a prophet's own lived story — whose later fulfillment is what testifies; it is expressly not a wonder performed on demand.", "consensus_core_identification": "A visible pointer to divine reality whose central case is the authenticating miracle/wonder that reveals God's power and Christ's identity and summons faith.", "book_core_identification": "A predictive prophecy (often enacted in a prophet's life) whose fulfillment over time is the testimony; the miraculous-wonder sense is explicitly demoted or excluded.", "core_relation": "BOOK_NARROWS", "extension_relation": "PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION", "boundary_disagreement": "The book excludes on-demand wonders and, implicitly, the freestanding miracle-as-sign from the category, while elevating what the consensus lists as secondary senses — the prophetic sign-act (Ezekiel as a sign), the predictive confirmatory sign (Isa 7:14), and the sign of Jonah — to the definitional center. Cases the consensus treats as paradigmatic (e.g., Johannine miracles as signs, Exodus plagues as authenticating wonders) are pushed to the margin or out of the category, while the prophecy-fulfillment cases the consensus treats as subsidiary become the whole definition.", "material_contradiction": "", "rationale": "Both readings retain the same general referent: something given by God that points beyond itself and testifies, calling for recognition and faith. The book does not replace this category; it relocates its center from 'miraculous act displaying power' to 'advance prophecy verified by fulfillment.' Every element of the book's definition appears within the consensus responses as an acknowledged sense — prophetic sign-acts (Isa 20:3; Ezek 4, 12, 24), confirmatory predictive signs (Isa 7:14; Exod 3:12), and the sign of Jonah with its rejection of sign-seeking (Matt 12:38-40; Luke 11:29-30). The book's 'not a wonder performed on demand' echoes the consensus's own negative sense (an evil generation seeks a sign). Because the central category survives while the boundary and paradigm cases are materially reshuffled — excluding some cases the consensus admits and promoting a subsidiary sense to primary — this is REFINED rather than DIVERGENT. It would be DIVERGENT only if the book denied that signs point to divine action at all or identified a wholly different referent.", "citation_support": "PARTIAL", "strongest_objection": "One could argue for DIVERGENT: the book's common-view note explicitly names the consensus reading ('a miraculous act pointing to God's power and Christ's identity') and its definition seems to reject it ('not a wonder performed on demand'), which reads as a replacement of the consensus's central identification, not a mere boundary adjustment — since the Johannine miracle-signs are the consensus's paradigm case and appear excluded. Conversely, a MATCH argument could note that the book merely foregrounds a sense every consensus response already lists. The REFINED verdict sits between these: the qualifier 'on demand' suggests the book rejects sign-seeking wonders rather than all miraculous signs, preserving the shared category while contesting its center of gravity.", "confidence": "medium"}
